full_judgment:
7. The High Court Division observed that the suit was not maintainable in view of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as (i) no consequential relief was sought. (ii) a registered deed carries a rebuttable presumption of authenticity, (iii) the plaintiff failed to prove that his father, the executant, was physically and mentally incapacitated to execute the deeds. 

 13. We are in full accord with the High Court Division so far as its observation on the rebuttable presumption of genuineness is concerned. The language in section 60 of the Registration Act is clear enough to dean that a registered document carries a strong presumption to the effect that the procedure was properly followed. Indeed that is what the Privy Council observed in the case of Purshotom Das (33 IA 60). 

 14. In similar vein, this Division in Abani Mohan vs. Asst. Custodian (SDO) of the Vested Property, Chandpur and others, 39 DLR (AD) 223, observed that if the question is whether the deed is genuine or not, the simple answer is, it being a registered document, is showered with a strong presumption as to genuineness Sections 59. 79 and 114 of the Evidence Act also lend support to Section 60 of the Registration Act on this score. No doubt, this presumption is rebuttable, which connotes that presumption raised by the admitted fact of registration could he rebutted by adducing countervailing evidence, showing that notwithstanding the fact of registration, the executant did not really affix his signature or thumb impression voluntarily which in the given circumstances, could be done by adducing expert evidence as to the physical and/or mental incapacity of the executant.
